The electricity access dataset

655 million

people live without electricity.

This page is one dataset and nothing else: every country on Earth, 1990–2024. It says who lacks electricity, where they are, which way each country is moving, and what the data cannot tell you.

Where the gap is largest

Nigeria, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda. These five hold 43 % of the world's unserved population.

+60 M

Where it is getting worse

21 countries had more people without power in 2024 than in 2010 — 17 of them in Africa. DR Congo alone added 25 million.

If you remember one country, remember DR Congo: the second-largest gap on Earth, and the only country that is both near the top and losing ground quickly.

Everything below is the same file read more carefully: where these numbers come from, how they moved, and the four things that limit what they can be used for.

The headline

The number, and how it changed

A halving in one generation is real. It also means half the problem is still there — and the rest of this page is about which half.

What progress looks like

Most of that progress has one country's name on it

420 → 1 450 914 India's count, 2000 to 2024 — a fall of 419 million.

China, Indonesia, Bangladesh and Vietnam did the same thing at smaller scale. The number responds when people are connected, and it responds quickly. That is what makes the next section the one that matters.

The turn

The world halved the problem. One region doubled its share.

−91%
outside Sub-Saharan Africa:
823 → 76
+14%
Sub-Saharan Africa:
506 → 579
Sub-Saharan Africa held 38% of the world's people without electricity in 2000. By 2024 it held 88%.

Africa did not collapse — its number rose 14%. Everywhere else improved so quickly that Africa's share of what remained went up anyway. This is the fact the headline number hides, and it is the single most consequential thing in the file.

Inside the region that holds 88 %

Sub-Saharan Africa is not one problem. Its five largest countries hold 49 % of the region's total, and 17 of its 48 countries reporting in 2024 went backwards between 2010 and 2024, together adding 59 people.

Two directions at once

The same twenty countries, by direction

Two different things can be true of a country at once: it can hold a very large number of people without electricity and be improving, or hold a large number and be getting worse. The chart below separates the two.

Both groups are real, and they are different problems. A country in the teal group has a large backlog and is working through it. A country in the red group has a large backlog that is growing — which means the supply side is losing ground to something else, most often population.

Going backwards

21 countries went backwards

21

+60

This is what it looks like when the population grows faster than the grid. The share of households with power can improve every year while the absolute number of people without it still rises. The Democratic Republic of Congo alone added 25 million.

At Sub-Saharan Africa's rate over the past 14 years, halving the region's number would take over 333 years.
The deadline

Where the trend points

509 million would still be without electricity in 2030, if every country keeps its recent pace — including the 21 currently moving backwards.

The fine print

What this data is — and what it cannot tell you

Everything on this page comes from a single file: data/people-without-electricity-country.csv. Four things decide how to read every number above.

7 140
rows
214
countries
35
years, 1990 to 2024
0
missing values

Four things to know before reading any number above

  • It counts connections, not reliable supply. A household with a meter that sits through daily blackouts counts here as having access. The number of people without dependable power is larger than anything on this page — and this file cannot measure it.
  • A zero means zero, not "missing". 49 countries report nobody without access in every year they appear. Dropping or imputing zeros would invent a problem the file says does not exist.
  • The file also contains 15 regional averages ("Sub-Saharan Africa", "World", income groups). They are useful for comparison but must never be counted alongside countries — the region and its members are both in the file, so mixing them double-counts people.
  • It stops at the country border. Electricity access is ultimately a village-level fact, and this file cannot see that far down.
What you can aim at

What this data lets you aim at — and what decides it

The file supports several different slices, and they point at different places. Which one is useful depends entirely on the criteria you bring; the data does not choose for you. These are the slices, side by side.

655 M

Largest numbers

Nigeria, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Tanzania, Uganda. The biggest backlogs in absolute terms. Twenty countries hold 78% of the total.

21

Getting worse

Countries where the number rose since 2010. DR Congo, Niger, Chad, Malawi, Mozambique, Somalia. 17 of the 21 are in Africa.

−91%

Already improving

Everything outside Sub-Saharan Africa. India, Bangladesh, China, Indonesia, and 120 countries that reduced their number since 2010.

88%

Concentrated

Sub-Saharan Africa's share of what remains — up from 38% in 2000. The problem has moved rather than shrunk.

What would decide between them

None of the following can be answered from this file. They are the questions that would narrow the list above to a place — and each needs a different source.

  • Reliable supply, not just a connection. This file cannot distinguish a household with steady power from one with a meter and a daily blackout. The addressable group is larger than anything on this page, and this file cannot size it.
  • Whether the area is off-grid at all. A village connected to a working grid is a different problem from one that has never been connected.
  • What it currently costs to supply. Diesel generation per kilowatt-hour is public for some countries and not others, and it changes the economics completely.
  • Whether there is a load that cannot wait. A health facility with a vaccine cold chain, or a water pump, changes what a solution has to guarantee. That is not in this file — it needs facility records.
  • Population and households. To know what a number means relative to a place, this file would need to be joined to census data.
This file can size a market. It cannot choose a site — and the criteria above, not the data, are what turn one into the other.
Questions

Questions, answered and not answered

Each question below is marked with whether this data answers it. Nothing is filled in with an opinion.

answered
Who exactly is affected?

At country level: 655 233 853 people in 2024. 88% of them in Sub-Saharan Africa. 78% of them in twenty countries. The largest single number is Nigeria, 87 254 810.

At the level of a person, no. This file has no sub-national data. It can say which country, never which town.

answered
How many people could a solution reach?

The file gives the size of the problem: 655 233 853 people. It cannot give the size of a reachable group, because that depends on criteria it does not contain — reliability, grid status, cost to serve. Any reach figure derived from this file alone would be the whole problem restated.

answered
Where is the problem getting worse rather than better?

21 countries, listed above, adding 60 people since 2010. 17 of the 21 are in Africa.

answered
Is progress possible?

Yes, and the file shows it happening. India went from 420 to 1 450 914. Outside Sub-Saharan Africa the total fell 91%. The world total halved in 24 years.

answered
Does the trend reach zero by 2030?

No. At the 2010–2024 pace, 509 people would remain. This is an extrapolation of an aggregate, not a forecast — it assumes every country holds its recent pace.

not answered
Which specific place should be targeted?

This file cannot answer it. It has no data below country level. Choosing a site requires criteria — grid status, cost to serve, presence of a critical load — that live in other sources. The section above lists them.

not answered
How reliable is the supply where people are connected?

Not measurable here. The indicator counts connection, so a household with a meter and daily blackouts is indistinguishable from one with steady power. Any claim about reliability needs a different dataset.

not answered
Who specifically benefits — which household, which facility?

Not in this file. Naming a person or a facility requires local records: health-facility lists, barangay or municipal registers, utility connection data. The file gives the country and the scale; everything below that is elsewhere.

If you read nothing else

The most important thing on this page

26%
of everyone without electricity lives in just two countries — Nigeria and DR Congo
88%
of what remains is in Sub-Saharan Africa, up from 38% in 2000
21
countries are moving backwards, adding 60 people since 2010
509 M
would still lack electricity in 2030 if the current pace holds
The world solved half of this problem in 24 years. The half that is left is not spread evenly — it is concentrated in Africa, concentrated in a few countries, and in those countries it is growing rather than shrinking.

That is the difference between a problem being solved and a problem being outpaced. India shows the first: 419 million people connected in 24 years. Nigeria and DR Congo show the second: their numbers went up over the same period, because population grew faster than the grid. Everything else on this page is detail around those two facts.

Source: data/people-without-electricity-country.csv (7 140 rows, 214 countries, 1990–2024). Regional figures are the World Bank regional aggregates carried in the same file.
